senses: A kind of ghost or spirit in Japanese folklore.
ety: From Japanese 式(しき)神(がみ) (shikigami).

senses: The edible fruit of these shrubs.
ety: From Middle English berberie, from Medieval Latin berberis (on which see Arabic بَرْبَارِيس (barbārīs)), influenced by berie (“berry”). Doublet of berberis and related to Berber.

senses: A clumsy, heavy, stupid, silly or blundering person.
ety: After Tony Lumpkin, an ignorant young man in Oliver Goldsmith's She Stoops to Conquer (1771; first performed 1773).

senses: Lactation (the secretion of milk from nipples) that is not associated with childbirth or nursing.
ety: From galacto- + -rrhea, from Ancient Greek γάλακτος (gálaktos, “milk”) + ῥέω /ῥοία (rhéō, “flow”).

senses: Resembling vomit in colour, texture, etc.
Inclined to vomit; sick.
Vile; contemptible.
ety: From puke + -y. Compare German Low German pukig (“sickly, unhealthy, ailing”).
examples: The walls in this abandoned waiting area were painted a pukey orange, compounding the feeling of queasiness I'd had since breakfast.
His heart was thumping harder than ever, and it was impossible to tell if the sickish, pukey feeling deep down in his belly was relief or terror.
There's no way he'd allow a dog on his couch or on his 500-thread-count sheets, let alone a pukey baby.

senses: A Spanish blood sausage, sometimes with rice and onions as ingredients.
An administrative unit of British Raj, consisting of a number of villages. Since Indian independence, replaced by the block or tahsil.
ety: From Urdu پَرَگْنَہ (paragna) (Hindi परगना (paragnā)), from Persian پرگنة.
examples: Many in the BJP, especially tribal leaders from the Santhal Pargana, blamed the crushing defeat against JMM on the CM's organisational skills.

senses: An official meeting or consultation.
The meeting of a government council, especially of an Italian, Spanish, or Portuguese government or agency.
The minutes or report of such a government council.
ety: From Italian consulta and Spanish consulta, attested in English since the eighteenth century. Doublet of consult.

senses: A thick Polish soup made from vegetable or meat broth, containing potatoes and barley groats.
A traditional alcoholic drink made from vodka (or other grain spirit) and honey, popular in Poland, Belarus, and Lithuania.
A yearly synagogue membership fee (in Western Sephardic communities)
The items of cloth used to make up a bed, such as sheets and pillowcases, formerly made of linen but now manufactured in a wide variety of material such as cotton or polyester.
The manufacture of things from biological materials.
Synonym of allocational (“of or pertaining to the allocation of resources”).
The replacement currency of the Austro-Hungarian krone in Hungary after World War I.
ety: From Hungarian korona. Doublet of corona, crown, koruna, krona, króna, and krone.

senses: A layer of hard clay subsoil or sedimentary rock; hardpan.
ety: From Spanish caliche, from Latin calx (“pebble”); compare chalk.

senses: Presently experiencing or having previously experienced menopause.
A fairy chess piece that moves one square orthogonally.
ety: Borrowed from Arabic وَزِير (wazīr, “helper, aide, minister”, literally “one who bears (the burden of office)”). Doublet of vizier.

senses: A case for the corporal cloth used in the Eucharist.
ety: From New Latin, from Latin thēca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “a case, box, receptacle”), from τίθημι (títhēmi, “put, set, place”). Doublet of tay.

senses: A walk or journey with no particular haste.
ety: Probably an alteration or variant of bumble (verb), perhaps influenced semantically by association with amble (verb). This term is originally nautical and military in usage, and is previously used outside the current meaning of traveling on foot.

senses: Synonym of mastersinger.
A traditional Japanese inn with communal baths and other public areas.
ety: From Japanese 旅館(りょかん) (ryokan), which is from Middle Chinese 旅館 (MC ljoX kwanH, “inn, traveller's lodge”). Compare modern Chinese 旅館／旅馆 (lǚguǎn, “hotel”), from 旅 (lǚ, “travel”) + 館／馆 (guǎn, “lodging-house”).
examples: Mr. Ducasse is pursuing plans for a new hotel one hour from central Tokyo, a cross between a ryokan, a traditional Japanese inn, and an auberge, a French country inn.

senses: The monetary unit of Tuscany from 1826 to 1859, subdivided into 100 quatrini; a florin.
Characterized by heavy or undesirably loud bass sounds.
examples: If you're miking a boomy acoustic, the proximity effect can work against you, but having it on a thin-sounding arch-top can work for you.
As an airliner approaches you from a long way off, the sound is first heard as rumble, and, as it get closer and then directly overhead, the sound becomes increasingly boomier.
For the third movement Mr. Safronov had Schubert’s piano sketch as a guide, but his big, boomy orchestration, with a gentle pastoral trio at its core, sounded jarring after the first two movements.

senses: To examine closely; to scrutinize.
ety: Possibly from Middle English pars (“parts, shares; parts of speech, grammar”), from Old French pars (plural of part (“part, portion, share”)), from Latin pars (“part, piece, share”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to carry forth; to sell”).

senses: A form of democracy in which decisions are made by a simple majority of some organized group.
A hard ball, similar in size to a baseball, used in hurling.
A tin mine or tinworks.
ety: From Late Latin stannaria, from Latin stannum (“tin”). By surface analysis, stann- + -ary.

senses: Sedges in the genera Bolboschoenus or Schoenoplectus (formerly considered Scirpus), having clusters of spikelets.
ety: From Middle English bulrish, perhaps from bule (“bull”) (in the sense of "large") + rish (“rush”).

senses: A box used to hold an artist's paints.
Computer hardware or software for creating or editing graphics.
examples: Nolan visits the Quantel computer laboratory to experiment with its vast digital paintbox.

senses: An issuer of a bill.
One who bills (caresses in fondness), in the context of billing and cooing.
The act or process of making something more complex.
examples: All this represents a change in American society, and a complexification of it.
In Elise Boulding's analysis, the conservative qualities of woman's mysteries chose not to keep pace with the complexification of urban life.
For rational beings will of course try simple things first and thereafter be driven step by step towards an ever enhanced complexification

senses: The act or process of sexualizing.
examples: We are inclined to doubt Pott's confident assumption that sexualization is a necessary consequence of personification.

senses: An intersection or roundabout, where tracks or roads cross (often used in place names).
A courtyard.
ety: From Hindi चौक (cauk, “plaza, square, courtyard”), from Sanskrit चतुष्क (catuṣka, “quadrangular courtyard, crossway”).

senses: A fabric of fine cotton muslin of Bengali origin, with coloured stripes and patterns.
A thick red Thai curry made with peanuts and spices.
A hundred-millionth (10⁻⁸) of a bitcoin; the same as 10 nanocoins (nBTC) or 10⁻⁸ BTC.
ety: Named after Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous designer of Bitcoin, from Japanese さとし (Satoshi), nominalization of the classical adjective 聡し (satoshi), modern 聡い (satoi, “clever, smart, sharp”).

senses: A sea slug belonging to the order Nudibranchia.
ety: Circa 19th century, borrowed from translingual Nudibranchia, from Latin nudus (“naked”) + branchia (“gills”).

senses: To make or render rich or richer.
To become rich or richer; become superior in quality, condition or effectiveness.
To gain richness; become heightened or intensified in brilliancy.
Someone from downtown.
examples: Mr. Jacobs continues to push the envelope, using heavy-knit cashmere on an old-mannish cardigan with so much thrift shop cred that only a downtowner would dare.
He began giving parties in a loft on Broadway at Houston Street, with artists, techies and other downtowners.

senses: Any of several lacewings of the family Chrysopidae.
Any of several flowering plants of the subtribe Helianthinae.
